Prussia: German state from 1525 to 1947. Prussia (German: Preußen [ˈpʁɔʏsn̩]; Old Prussian: Prūsija) was a German state centred on the North European Plain.
A Bosnian Serb commander of the Army of Republika Srpska during the Yugoslav Wars, he's now serving a life sentence in The Hague for genocide and crimes against humanity — who is he?
This American author built a personal-finance empire around his bestselling Rich Dad Poor Dad book series, even as one of his companies filed for bankruptcy in 2012 — who is he?
Robert Kiyosaki: American finance author and investor (born 1947)
An Iraqi politician who served as the fifth president from 1979 until his overthrow in 2003 during the US-led invasion, previously a vice president and prime minister—who was he?
Saddam Hussein: President of Iraq from 1979 to 2003. The policies and ideologies he championed are collectively known as Saddamism, a right-wing variant of Ba'athism.
This Sanskrit term, meaning 'wandering' or 'running around in circles,' describes the ongoing cycle of life, death, and rebirth central to Indian religious philosophy — what is it called?
Saṃsāra: Indian concept of the cyclical process of death and rebirth.
Daughter of Bangladesh's first president, she became the country's longest-serving prime minister and one of the world's longest-serving female heads of government — who is she?
Sheikh Hasina: Prime Minister of Bangladesh (1996–2001; 2009–2024)
Established as a client state of Nazi Germany in March 1939, this Central European nation's army also joined the invasion of Poland that year — which state, whose capital was Bratislava?
Slovak Republic (1939–1945): Client state of Nazi Germany. The Slovak part of Czechoslovakia declared independence with German support one day before the German occupation of Bohemia and Moravia.
It's the season when the earliest sunrises and latest sunsets crowd around a single solstice — and when half the planet swelters, the other half shivers. Which season is it?
Summer: Hottest of the four temperate seasons.
Instituted by Diocletian in AD 293, this system split rule of the Roman Empire between two senior 'augusti' and two junior 'caesars' — what was it called?
Tetrarchy: Roman system of power division among four rulers.
A former Army officer, this Arkansas Republican unseated incumbent Mark Pryor in 2014 to become the state's junior U.S. senator — who is he?
Tom Cotton: American politician and veteran (born 1977)
Symbolizing both a diamond's indestructibility and a thunderbolt's force, this ritual scepter-like tool is used alongside a bell in Tibetan Buddhist ceremonies — what is it called?
Vajra: Spiritual weapon or symbol in Dharmic religions.
A key figure of Chile's Nueva Canción movement, this singer-songwriter was arrested and killed in the days following the 1973 coup that overthrew President Allende — who was he?
Víctor Jara: Chilean folk singer and activist (1932–1973)

Serving four non-consecutive terms as British Prime Minister between 1868 and 1894 — more than anyone else — this Liverpool-born statesman began as a Conservative MP before becoming the face of the Liberal Party — who was he?
Born in Georgia, this Red Army officer and engineer was the eldest son of a Bolshevik revolutionary who became head of the Soviet Union — who is he?
Yakov Dzhugashvili: Red Army officer and Joseph Stalin's son (1907–1943)
An early convert to Islam and a commander at the Battle of Badr in 624, this Arab Muslim general fought in the Ridda Wars and the early conquests of Persia, Syria and North Africa — who was he?
Zubayr ibn al-Awwam: Arab Muslim military commander (594–656)
Which of these four is the eldest?
Eratosthenes (born 276 BC) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these was born first?
Georges Dumézil (born 1898) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these people was born first?
Ada Lovelace (born 1815) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below was established earliest?

Lisp (programming language) (founded 1958) is the earliest of the four. Originally specified in the late 1950s, it is the second-oldest high-level programming language still in common use, after Fortran.
Which of these four appeared first?
Pascal (programming language) (published 1972) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is a physicist?
Pierre Curie is a physicist. Pierre Curie (15 May 1859 – 19 April 1906) was a French physicist and chemist, and a pioneer in crystallography and magnetism.
Which of these four is a chemist?
Mario Molina is a chemist. Mario José Molina-Pasquel Henríquez (19 March 1943 – 7 October 2020) was a Mexican physical chemist.
What is the atomic number of Hydrogen?
Hydrogen is a chemical element; it has the symbol H and atomic number 1.
In what year was Hans Albert Einstein born?
Hans Albert Einstein (May 14, 1904 – July 26, 1973) was a Swiss-American engineer, the second child and first son of physicists Albert Einstein and Mileva Marić.
In what year was Mahmoud Ahmadinejad born?
Mahmoud Ahmadinejad (né Sabbaghian; born 28 October 1956) is an Iranian politician who served as the sixth president of Iran from 2005 to 2013.
In what year was Kitty O'Neil born?
Kitty O'Neil: O'Neil subsequently moved into car racing and became a pioneering woman in the stunt industry in Hollywood.
In what year did Blaise Pascal die?
Blaise Pascal (19 June 1623 – 19 August 1662) was a French mathematician, physicist, inventor, philosopher, and Catholic writer.
In what year did Milton Friedman die?
Milton Friedman: Friedman's challenges to what he called "naive Keynesian theory" began with his interpretation of consumption, which tracks how consumers spend.
In what year was Penicillin discovered?
Penicillin was discovered in 1928 by the Scottish physician Alexander Fleming as a crude extract of P. rubens.
In what year was Coulomb's law discovered?
Coulomb's law: This electric force is conventionally called the electrostatic force or Coulomb force.
Which company manufactures Eurocopter AS350 Écureuil?
Eurocopter AS350 Écureuil: Airbus Helicopters. The AS355 Ecureuil 2 is a twin-engine variant, marketed in North America as the TwinStar.
In which country is Junkers Ju 52?
Junkers Ju 52: Germany. Development of the Ju 52 commenced in the late 1920s, headed by German aeronautical engineer Ernst Zindel.
Who is credited with discovering Indium?
Indium: Ferdinand Reich. Indium is a chemical element; its symbol is In and its atomic number is 49.
Who is credited with discovering Californium?
Californium: Stanley Gerald Thompson. Californium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Cf and atomic number 98.
Who is credited with discovering Fluorine?
Fluorine: Henri Moissan. Fluorine is a chemical element; it has symbol F and atomic number 9.
This is the most common genetic cause of dwarfism, typically producing short arms and legs with a normal-length torso and an enlarged head with a prominent forehead — what condition is it?
Achondroplasia is a genetic disorder whose primary feature is dwarfism.
The twelfth-brightest star in our night sky and the brightest in the constellation Aquila. It's one of the three vertices of the Summer Triangle asterism. Name this star.

Altair is the brightest star in the equatorial constellation of Aquila and the twelfth-brightest star in the night sky. It has the Bayer designation Alpha Aquilae, which is Latinised from α Aquilae and abbreviated Alpha Aql or α Aql.
Whether contracted through the skin, the lungs, or the gut, this Bacillus-driven infection can take up to two months to show symptoms — what is it?
Anthrax is an infection caused by the bacterium Bacillus anthracis or Bacillus cereus biovar anthracis.
First described in 1740, this flowering-plant family rivals only the orchid family in sheer number of species, with over 32,000 recognized today — what family is it?
Asteraceae is a large family of flowering plants that consists of over 32,000 known species in over 1,900 genera within the order Asterales.
Designed to replace the aging Tu-126 'Moss,' this Soviet early-warning aircraft saw only about 42 built before the USSR's breakup ended production in 1992 — what is it?
Beriev A-50 (NATO reporting name: Mainstay) is a Soviet-origin airborne early warning and control (AEW&C) aircraft that is based on the Ilyushin Il-76 transport plane.
Every subatomic particle is either this integer-spin class or a fermion; Paul Dirac named the class after physicist Satyendra Nath Bose, whose statistics they obey — what's the class called?
Boson is a subatomic particle whose spin quantum number has an integer value (0, 1, 2,...).
Produced when quicklime is mixed with water, this white, powdery compound goes by many names in industry and food prep, where it's labeled E526 — what compound is it?
Calcium hydroxide (traditionally called slaked lime) is an inorganic compound with the chemical formula Ca(OH)2.
Retired from Istanbul Technical University, this geologist holds foreign membership in both the US and Russian National Academies of Sciences. Who is he?
Celâl Şengör (born 24 March 1955) is a Turkish geologist.

This genus of flowering trees and shrubs, native to South and East Asia, Melanesia, and Australia, gave rise through extensive hybridization to oranges, lemons, grapefruits, and limes — what's the genus called?
Citrus is a genus of flowering trees and shrubs in the family Rutaceae.

What zoological term describes the internal-fertilization mating behavior in which a male animal introduces sperm directly into a female's reproductive tract — occurring via a 'cloacal kiss' in birds and most reptiles, or vaginally in mammals?
Copulation (zoology) is animal sexual behavior in which a male introduces sperm into the female's body, especially directly into the female's reproductive tract.
This Canadian-born entrepreneur co-founded a company later acquired by MSC Software in 1998, then went on to co-found and lead a massively popular online gaming and creation platform — who is he?
David Baszucki (buh-; born January 20, 1963) is a Canadian-born American entrepreneur, engineer, and software developer.
This Penn professor's discoveries about modified nucleosides made the Pfizer and Moderna COVID-19 vaccines possible, earning him a share of the 2023 Nobel Prize in Medicine — who is he?
Drew Weissman (born September 7, 1959) is an American physician and immunologist known for his contributions to RNA biology.

Named for Latin words meaning 'within the cytoplasm' and 'little net,' this eukaryotic cell organelle handles protein folding and comes in rough and smooth varieties, forming an interconnected network of membrane-enclosed sacs — name this organelle?
Endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a part of a transportation system of the eukaryotic cell, and has many other important functions such as protein folding.
Cats in this subfamily can purr but never roar, thanks to a bony rather than flexible hyoid bone — which subfamily?
Felinae are a subfamily of the Felidae distinguished by a bony hyoid, because of which they can purr but not roar.

Found from the tropics to subarctic regions and accounting for about 88% of living amphibian species, this tailless, semiaquatic creature has a name that informally splits into 'toad' for the warty ones — what is it?
Frog is any member of a diverse and largely semiaquatic group of short-bodied, tailless amphibian vertebrates composing the order Anura (coming from the Ancient Greek, literally 'without tail').
This ancient metabolic pathway breaks glucose down into pyruvate through ten enzyme-catalyzed reactions in a cell's cytosol, generating ATP along the way. What process is it?
Glycolysis is the metabolic pathway that converts glucose (C6H12O6) into pyruvate and, in most organisms, occurs in the liquid part of cells (the cytosol).
Hailed by Time as a 2019 'Pioneer' yet condemned as a mad scientist, which Chinese biophysicist announced in 2018 that he'd created the first gene-edited human babies?
He Jiankui (pinyin: H Jinku HUH KWAY; born 1984) is a Chinese biophysicist known for his controversial first use of genome editing in humans in 2018.
One of the six Celtic nations, this peninsula in northwest France was known as Armorica under Roman rule before becoming an independent kingdom and later a duchy. What region is it?
Hydra (genus) is a genus of small freshwater hydrozoans in the phylum Cnidaria.
An ISO standard defines it as "a new or changed entity, realizing or redistributing value" — and it's related to, but not the same as, invention. What word are we after?
Innovation is the practical implementation of ideas that result in the creation or improvements of goods or services.
A former Chicago financial options trader, this internet entrepreneur co-founded a nonprofit free encyclopedia as well as the for-profit wiki host Fandom — who is he?
Jimmy Wales (born August 8, 1966) is an American and British internet entrepreneur and former financial trader.
This American biologist and one-time Communist Party member had four husbands, the last being the physicist who led Los Alamos — who was she?
Kitty Oppenheimer (ne Puening; August 8, 1910 - October 27, 1972) was an American biologist, botanist, and a member of the Communist Party of America until leaving in the 1930s.
This Chinese herbalist, martial artist, and tactical advisor died in 1933 claiming a birth year of 1677 — a longevity claim gerontologists now regard as myth — who was he?
Li Ching-Yuen (simplified; traditional; pinyin: L Qngyn, died 6 May 1933) was a Chinese herbalist, martial artist and tactical advisor, known for his supposed extreme longevity.
Caused by a compromised lymphatic system, this condition raises infection risk in affected tissue and is treated with compression and massage rather than water pills — what is it?
Lymphedema (USA), lymphoedema (UK) also known as lymphatic edema (US)/oedema (UK), is a condition of localized swelling caused by a compromised lymphatic system.
Among the first women in Canada to earn a medical doctorate, this physician-chemist is best remembered for a landmark 1913 enzyme-kinetics paper co-authored with Leonor Michaelis — who was she?
Maud Menten (March 20, 1879 - July 17, 1960) was a Canadian physician and chemist.

This large-scale industrial activity extracts everything from coal and gemstones to rock salt and potash from the Earth, providing raw materials that can't be grown or feasibly manufactured — what is this activity called?
Mining is the extraction of geological materials and minerals from Earth's surface.
Named from the Ancient Greek for 'mouse's ear' after its foliage's shape, this genus of small blue Northern Hemisphere flowers serves as Alaska's official state flower — what's the genus?
Myosotis is a genus of flowering plants in the borage family Boraginaceae.
Containing turbinates and olfactory mucosa within its cavity, this organ centers the human face and provides an alternate airway while infants nurse — which body part?
Nose is a sensory organ and respiratory structure in vertebrates.
This bivalve mollusk is prized both as a delicacy on the half shell and, in certain species, for the pearls it produces inside its shell — what is it?
Oyster is the common name for a number of different families of salt-water bivalve molluscs that live in marine or brackish habitats.
Named from Greek words for 'odd' and 'toe,' this mammalian order groups horses, rhinoceroses, and tapirs together based on their toe count. Which order?
Perissodactyla (from Ancient Greek, perisss 'odd' and, dktylos 'finger, toe'), or odd-toed ungulates, is an order of ungulates.
A member of the cashew family and a priority tree-nut allergen, this green seed saw the US, Iran, and Turkey produce 87% of the world's 1.4 million tonnes in 2024 — what is it?
Pistachio (UK also; Pistacia vera) is a small to medium-sized tree of the cashew family.
Split into the strepsirrhines — lemurs and lorisids — and the haplorhines — tarsiers, monkeys and apes — this order ranges in size down to tiny Madame Berthe's — what is it?

Primate is an order of mammals, which is further divided into the strepsirrhines, which include lemurs, galagos, and lorisids; and the haplorhines, which include tarsiers and simians (monkeys and apes).

Founding an organization promoting swadeshi economics against globalization, this Indian social activist later allied with a yoga guru to combine that economic message with the promotion of yoga and Ayurveda — who is he?
Rajiv Dixit (30 November 1967 - 30 November 2010) was an Indian social activist who founded the Azadi Bachao Andolan.

This long-term skin condition causes facial redness, pimples, and swelling, and can lead to a severely enlarged, reddened nose in extreme cases — its exact cause remains unknown — name this condition?
Rosacea is a long-term skin condition that typically affects the face.

Native to the North Pacific coasts, this marine mammal is the heaviest member of the weasel family yet one of the smallest marine mammals, insulated by the densest fur coat in the animal kingdom — what is it?
Sea otter (Enhydra lutris) is a marine mammal native to the coasts of the northern and eastern North Pacific Ocean.
Which urban model uses digital technology and data from citizens, buildings, and cameras to improve sustainability, efficiency, and social inclusion?
Smart city is an urban model that leverages technology, human capital, and governance to improve sustainability, efficiency, and social inclusion, which are considered goals for cities of the future.
Known by his online username 'spez,' this web developer co-founded an airfare search engine before leading the world's seventh most-visited website as CEO — who is he?
Steve Huffman (born 1983 or 1984), also known by his Reddit username spez, is an American web developer and entrepreneur.
Every part of this Old World evergreen tree is poisonous except the fleshy red covering around its seed, and it's native across Eurasia and Northwest Africa — what tree species is it?
Taxus baccata is an Old World species of evergreen tree in the family Taxaceae.
Tetrapods have these digits at the end of each limb; horses walk on their very tips in what's called an unguligrade stance — what are they?
Toe are the digits of the foot of a tetrapod.
Native to boreal forests and Arctic tundra across the Northern Hemisphere, this small evergreen heath-family shrub produces edible berries central to Nordic cuisine — what plant is it?
Vaccinium vitis-idaea is a small evergreen shrub in the heath family, Ericaceae. It is known colloquially as the lingonberry, partridgeberry, foxberry, mountain cranberry, or cowberry.
The first person to ever call himself a psychologist, this German founder of modern psychology launched Philosophische Studien, the field's first academic research journal — who is he?
Wilhelm Wundt (16 August 1832 - 31 August 1920) was a German physiologist, philosopher, professor, and one of the fathers of modern psychology.
Also called the belly, this body region sits between the chest and pelvis and is known as the metasoma in arthropods — which body part?
Abdomen: Part of the body between the chest and pelvis. The area occupied by the abdomen is called the abdominal cavity.

Now built by Leonardo but originally developed jointly by an Italian and an American helicopter maker, this 15-seat medium twin-engine helicopter serves VIP transport, firefighting, and search-and-rescue roles — which aircraft?
De Havilland Canada DHC-6 Twin Otter
AgustaWestland AW139: Twin-engined, medium-lift helicopter manufactured by Leonardo.

Believed to be an autoimmune attack on the immune privilege of hair follicles, this condition typically leaves a few coin-sized bald spots — and in rare cases takes every hair on the body. What's it called?
Alopecia areata: Medical condition. Alopecia areata (AA), also known as spot baldness, is a condition in which hair is lost from some or all areas of the body.
This English mathematician earned a knighthood and the Abel Prize for proving Fermat's Last Theorem, a problem that fascinated him since childhood in Nigeria. Who is he?
Andrew Wiles: British mathematician who proved Fermat's Last Theorem.
This inflammatory condition causes right lower abdominal pain and is commonly triggered by a blockage from a calcified mass of feces called a fecalith — what is it?

Often called a 'collapsed lung' in casual speech, this condition is really the partial deflation of the lung's alveoli rather than fluid filling them, and shows up frequently on chest X-rays — what is it?
Atelectasis: Partial collapse of a lung causing reduced gas exchange.
A tender herb of the mint family native from Central Africa to Southeast Asia, its Genovese or 'sweet' variety is a kitchen staple worldwide — what is it?
Basil: Culinary herb. Basil (Ocimum basilicum), also called great basil, is a culinary herb of the family Lamiaceae (mints).

Named after two French physicists who discovered it in 1820, this equation in magnetostatics relates a magnetic field to the strength, direction, and distance of an electric current — which physics rule?
Biot–Savart law: Law of classical electromagnetism.
This rigid organ not only supports the body and enables movement but also manufactures both red and white blood cells and stores essential minerals — what is it?
Bone: Rigid organs of the skeleton of vertebrates.

Marketed as Wellbutrin, this atypical antidepressant doubles as a stop-smoking aid and stands out for not causing sexual dysfunction or weight gain — what is this norepinephrine-dopamine reuptake inhibitor?
Bupropion: Medication mainly used for depression and smoking cessation.
This golden fungus — also known as 'girolle' — is often confused with a poisonous lookalike, though it remains a prized edible mushroom and the type species of its genus — which one is it?
Cantharellus cibarius: Species of fungus. Despite its characteristic features, C. cibarius can be confused with species such as the poisonous Omphalotus illudens.
Marketed as Zinacef and used against everything from meningitis to Lyme disease, this second-generation cephalosporin antibiotic was patented in 1971 — which drug?
Cefuroxime: Antibiotic medication. It is used by mouth or by injection into a vein or muscle.

Caused by a bacterium and often symptomless for weeks after exposure, this sexually transmitted infection can lead to pelvic inflammatory disease and infertility in women if untreated — which infection?
Chlamydia: Sexually transmitted bacterial infection. Chlamydia, or more specifically a chlamydia infection, is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis.
Native to Indonesia's Maluku Islands, these aromatic flower buds flavor your food but also turn up in toothpaste and soaps — what spice are they?
Clove: Spice made from flower buds.
Spanning information theory and cryptography at one end and hardware design at the other, this field is broadly described as the study of computation, information, and automation — what is it?
Computer science: Study of computation. Algorithms and data structures are central to computer science.
Originating in French cuisine and beloved in Spain, this breaded, deep-fried roll often reuses leftover roasted chicken or broth meat as its filling — what is it called?

The world's first commercial jet airliner, this sleek British craft tucked four turbojets into its wing roots — only for three to be lost in catastrophic mid-flight accidents within a year of entering service. Which aircraft?
De Havilland Comet: First commercial jet airliner, four-engined. The de Havilland DH.106 Comet is a four-engine narrow body aircraft developed and manufactured by de Havilland in the United Kingdom.
Formed when two simple sugar molecules join via a glycosidic bond, sucrose, lactose, and maltose all belong to this class of 'double sugars' — what is it called?
Disaccharide: Complex sugar. A disaccharide (also called a double sugar or biose) is the sugar formed when two monosaccharides are joined by glycosidic linkage.
This social science splits into a 'micro' branch studying individual agents and markets and a 'macro' branch treating whole economies as systems of production and consumption — what's the field?
Economics: Social science studying goods and services.
In this concept, a random variable's average uncertainty is measured by how much data is needed, on average, to describe which outcome occurred. What is this quantity called?

Entropy (information theory): Average uncertainty in variable's states. The choice of base for 
 
 
 
 log
 
 
 {\displaystyle \log }, the logarithm, varies for different applications.
With a cinnamon body, black-and-white wings, and a tall erectile crest, this widespread bird announces itself with a soft 'oop-oop-oop' call — what is it?
Eurasian hoopoe: Species of bird. The Eurasian hoopoe or common hoopoe (Upupa epops) is the most widespread species of hoopoe.
This centuries-old number theory statement claims there are no positive whole-number solutions to a^n + b^n = c^n whenever the exponent exceeds two — what's it called?
Fermat's Last Theorem: 17th-century conjecture proved by Andrew Wiles in 1994.
Part of the rose family and prized for fruit that ranges from very sweet to notably tart, this genus's garden hybrid is an important commercial crop worldwide — which genus is it?
One of Maxwell's equations, this application of the divergence theorem connects electric charge distribution to the electric field it creates. Which one is it?
Gauss's law: Foundational law of electromagnetism relating electric field and charge distributions.
Occurring in the cytosol, this ten-step metabolic pathway breaks glucose down into pyruvate while generating ATP and NADH — what process is it?
Glycolysis: Series of interconnected biochemical reactions.
After a record 43 years as crown prince, this Swedish monarch approved constitutional reforms stripping the crown of its remaining political powers shortly before his 1973 death. Who was he?
Gustaf VI Adolf: King of Sweden from 1950 to 1973.
In their normal state these vascular cushions in the anal canal actually help with stool control; only when swollen or inflamed do they become the condition also known as piles — what is it?
Hemorrhoid: Vascular structures in the anal canal. The signs and symptoms of hemorrhoids depend on the type present.
Damage to the sympathetic trunk nerves produces this trio of symptoms on one side of the face — a constricted pupil, a droopy eyelid, and reduced sweating — what is this condition called?
Horner's syndrome: Facial disorder due to damage of the sympathetic nerves.
Marked in its severe stage by hallucinations and paradoxical undressing, which condition is defined as a body core temperature below 35 degrees Celsius?
Hypothermia: Human body core temperature below 35 °C (95 °F)
Known historically as green vitriol or copperas, this blue-green heptahydrate salt is used to treat anemia and forms a paramagnetic octahedral complex in water — which compound?
Iron(II) sulfate: Chemical compound. Iron(II) sulfate or ferrous sulfate (British English: sulphate instead of sulfate) denotes a range of salts with the formula FeSO4·xH2O.
Son of Taiwanese immigrants, this engineer launched the world's most valuable company from a Denny's restaurant in 1993 after earning a Stanford master's degree — who is he?
Jensen Huang: Taiwanese and American businessman (born 1963)
Sometimes grown just for looks, this cabbage relative's leaves can be bumpy, curly, or flat, in colors from purple to green — what leafy vegetable is it?
Kale: Form of cabbage with green or purple leaves.
Born of Peranakan Chinese cuisine, this spicy Southeast Asian noodle dish is often served in a rich coconut-curry soup soured with tamarind — what is it?
Laksa: Spicy noodle dish from Southeast Asia.
The offspring of a male lion and a female tiger, which hybrid cat is the largest of all living felines and — unlike its reverse-cross cousin — grows larger than either parent?
Liger: Lion and tigress hybrid. The liger is a hybrid offspring of a male lion (Panthera leo) and a tigress, or female tiger (Panthera tigris).

With nearly 5,000 species, these wingless parasitic insects spend their whole lives on a single warm-blooded host, either chewing skin and feathers or piercing the skin to feed on blood — what are they?
Louse: Infraorder of insects. Louse (pl.: lice) is the common name for any member of the infraorder Phthiraptera, which contains nearly 5,000 species of wingless parasitic insects.
Nicknamed the 'tree of death' and 'beach apple,' this small-fruited tropical tree oozes a milky sap so toxic it can blister skin on contact — which tree?
Manchineel: Poisonous plant from tropical North and South America.
This cone-shaped part of the brainstem controls involuntary functions from sneezing to heart rate, and was once known simply as 'the bulb' — which structure?
Medulla oblongata: Structure of the brain stem.
This scientific field studies microorganisms such as bacteria, fungi, and protists, encompassing sub-disciplines like virology and mycology — which discipline?

Thought to enjoy 'hybrid vigor' and a reduced risk of inbreeding-linked health problems, this catch-all term covers roughly 150 million dogs worldwide that don't belong to any officially recognized breed — what's it called?
This arthropod subphylum includes millipedes and centipedes, and one of its earliest fossils preserves the first known evidence of animals breathing air on land. What's the group called?
Myriapoda: Subphylum of arthropods. The group contains about 13,000 species, all of them terrestrial.
This Serbian-American engineer designed the modern alternating current electricity supply system—the backbone of today's power grid. Who?
Nikola Tesla: Serbian-American engineer and inventor (1856–1943)

This family of 138 primate species — including baboons, macaques, and mandrills — split off from a separate lineage of primates some 45 to 55 million years ago, yet is the closer kin to apes of the two — which family?
Old World monkey: Family of mammals. Old World monkey genera include baboons (genus Papio), red colobus (genus Piliocolobus), and macaques (genus Macaca).
A pale-blue gas with a chlorine-like pungent odour, this unstable three-atom cousin of oxygen forms by UV light and electrical discharges and shields us high in the stratosphere — what is it?
Nicknamed "javelina" or "skunk pig," this social New World mammal travels in herds called squadrons and counts true pigs as its closest living relatives — what pig-like ungulate is it?
This anxiety disorder involves an irrational, excessive fear that persists more than six months and can trigger fainting in blood-or-injury cases — what is it?
Phobia: Anxiety disorder classified by a persistent and excessive fear of an object or situation.
First synthesized in 1940 by bombarding uranium-238 with deuterons at UC Berkeley, this radioactive metal can expand up to 70% in volume when its surface oxidizes — which element?
Plutonium: Chemical element with atomic number 94 (Pu)
Though often mistaken for a true antelope, this hoofed North American mammal is actually the last living member of its own family, and its closest relatives are the giraffe and okapi — which animal?

Pronghorn: Species of North American hoofed mammal. The pronghorn (UK:, US:) (Antilocapra americana) is a species of artiodactyl (even-toed, hoofed) mammal indigenous to interior western and central North America.
Named for its four heads, this large muscle group covers the front of the thigh and is the sole muscle that extends the knee — what is it?
Quadriceps: Group of human leg muscle.

Also known as Willis–Ekbom disease, this neurological disorder creates an overwhelming urge to move one's limbs, especially when at rest, often described as a crawling or tingling sensation — what's the condition called?
Restless legs syndrome: Medical condition. There is often an unpleasant feeling in the legs that improves temporarily by moving them.
Also known as sixth disease, this childhood viral infection typically strikes before age three with a sudden fever followed by a pink rash lasting under three days — what's the condition called?
Roseola: Human disease caused by human herpesviruses.
This Indian-American executive became CEO of a major tech company in 2014, succeeding Steve Ballmer, after leading its cloud and enterprise division — who is he?
In this biological process, haploid gametes such as sperm and egg cells combine to form a zygote that develops into a diploid organism — what is it called?
Sexual reproduction: Biological process. Sexual reproduction is the most common life cycle in multicellular eukaryotes, such as animals, fungi and plants.

Once extracted from the ashes of certain salt-absorbing plants and now produced from ordinary salt and limestone via the Solvay process, this alkaline compound is also known as washing soda or soda ash — what is it?
Sodium carbonate: Chemical compound. Sodium carbonate (also known as washing soda, soda ash, sal soda, and soda crystals) is the inorganic compound with the formula Na2CO3 and its various hydrates.
Known for a synchronized aerial swarming display called murmuration, this glossy-plumed bird family includes talkative mynas as members — which birds?
